title: Progressive Memory Transformer: Memory-Aware Attention for Time-Series
claim: Sequence structure exists at several nested scales, and exposing intermediate representations allows direct supervision at each scale rather than only a global readout.
layout: Single wide panel, bottom-to-top hierarchy over a time axis, shaded receptive-field regions
description: A wide single-panel diagram of a three-level hierarchy over a time series. The bottom row, labeled Signal, is a wiggly curve whose segments alternate green and purple, with a time arrow t at the right. Above it, the Low row has a long line of small squares colored green or purple to match the signal. Gray lines group every three Low tokens into one Mid-level square, and some Mid squares are half green and half purple. Pink arrows run left to right between Mid squares. Higher up, Mid squares link to a few orange High-level squares joined by pink arrows. Each square has a pink circle attached, labeled Representation or State. Pink circles at the far right mark the Readout. Two shaded blobs, orange and yellow, mark receptive fields that grow with level. A gray rectangle highlights the exposed intermediate levels. The eye goes first to the colored token grid and the pink arrows.
caption: An illustration of the three levels of representation and how they capture distinct structural patterns. Shaded regions indicate expanding receptive fields. Exposing the intermediate representations (gray background) enables direct supervision at multiple scales, unlike standard global readouts.
abstract: Time-series carry structure simultaneously at multiple scales (fine-grained variation, mid-range motifs, and global properties) and downstream tasks operate at correspondingly different scales. Most existing self-supervised learning approaches supervise representations globally via instance-level contrastive losses and limited temporal neighborhood supervision, but do not explicitly exploit the structural hierarchy. We propose a learning framework that explicitly enforces a structural hierarchy across three scales independently: a local objective for token alignment, a mid-range objective for window-level motifs, and a global objective for sequence-level agreement. Realizing this framework requires the backbone to expose a representation at each scale; we introduce \textbf{Progressive Memory Transformer} (PMT), which augments a transformer with writable, window-aligned memory that exposes the mid-range scale alongside the token and sequence-level representations conventional transformers already provide. Across eight UCR/UEA/UCI classification benchmarks, a cue-retention probe, and forecasting benchmarks, PMT learns representations that probe well at the global, mid-range, and local scales---strong low-label classification (1--5\% labels), competitive forecasting performance across multiple horizons, and quantitative and qualitative evidence that memory states capture mid-range motifs.
